section_summary: This section traces State Department handling of Japanese and other Axis press representatives from a 1940 visa dispute involving journalist Toichiro Takamatsu through the wartime detention, exchange, and repatriation arrangements that followed Pearl Harbor. It includes reciprocal-treatment negotiations conducted through Switzerland and Spain, records concerning Japanese correspondents held at Hot Springs and Missoula, and Clarke H. Kawakami's public condemnation of Japan's attack. The later papers concern Kyozo Mori's automobile and personal property, Toshio Tomomatsu's proposed repatriation, and the disposition of European Axis nationals attached to official exchange parties.

subfiles.title: Telegram from London concerning Toichiro Takamatsu's visa application
subfiles.about: Requests instructions on a visa for Japanese journalist Toichiro Takamatsu, who wished to travel to the United States aboard a Japanese evacuation ship.
subfiles.summary: Takamatsu sought to cover the evacuation ship leaving Galway and possibly take a journalistic post at the Osaka Mainichi's New York office. The telegram describes his work for the Tokyo Nichi Nichi and gives Fukumichi Fukumoto as a New York reference.

subfiles.title: Duplicate of the October 15 Takamatsu telegram
subfiles.about: Duplicates the request for instructions on Takamatsu's proposed journey to the United States.
subfiles.summary: The copy repeats that Takamatsu hoped to travel on a Japanese evacuation ship and await a possible New York assignment. It again identifies his Tokyo Nichi Nichi background and Fukumichi Fukumoto as his reference.

subfiles.title: Second duplicate of the October 15 Takamatsu telegram
subfiles.about: Provides another duplicate of the London Embassy's Takamatsu visa inquiry.
subfiles.summary: Despite degraded OCR, the page repeats the same account of Takamatsu's planned departure from Galway and possible Osaka Mainichi employment in New York. It asks the Department to instruct the Embassy.

subfiles.title: Departmental refusal to authorize Takamatsu's visa
subfiles.about: Declines to authorize a visa because Takamatsu had not shown a legitimate reason to enter the United States.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that no visa should be issued on the facts presented. It indicates that the case could be reconsidered if Takamatsu received a definite work assignment in the United States.

subfiles.title: Copy of October 15 London telegram concerning Takamatsu
subfiles.about: Restates Takamatsu's request to travel to the United States and seek a New York newspaper assignment.
subfiles.summary: The copy says Takamatsu intended to cover a Japanese evacuation vessel departing Galway. It summarizes his Tokyo Nichi Nichi career and supplies Fukumichi Fukumoto's New York address.

subfiles.title: Additional copy of October 15 London telegram concerning Takamatsu
subfiles.about: Provides an additional file copy of the initial Takamatsu visa request.
subfiles.summary: The document repeats Takamatsu's plan to sail from Galway and possibly work for the Osaka Mainichi in New York. It also repeats his professional history and reference.

subfiles.title: Urgent telegram on Takamatsu's imminent departure
subfiles.about: Reports that Takamatsu had arranged to leave England on November 1 and urgently requests instructions.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy follows up its October 15 telegram because the applicant's departure was imminent. The message is marked rush and chargeable to the interested party.

subfiles.title: Letter reviewing the Takamatsu visa decision
subfiles.about: Explains the Department's visa instructions and notes that Takamatsu apparently sailed before receiving authorization.
subfiles.summary: The letter recounts the November 6 instruction to London that a visa was not authorized without a legitimate reason for travel, although a definite assignment could justify reconsideration. It notes that Takamatsu apparently sailed from Galway and says the Department had no authority to issue a visa without further information.

subfiles.title: Japanese Embassy request for a transit visa for Takamatsu
subfiles.about: Requests a transit visa after Takamatsu sailed from Galway aboard the Fushimi Maru and was recalled to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Miyazaki explains that Takamatsu chose the Japanese vessel to avoid the greater danger of naval attack on a British ship. Because Tokyo had recalled him, the Embassy withdrew its earlier request for a temporary visitor's visa and instead sought transit permission allowing about three weeks for travel from the East Coast to the West Coast.

subfiles.title: Japanese Embassy memorandum seeking expedited issuance of Takamatsu's visa
subfiles.about: Asks the Department to expedite a temporary visitor's visa before Takamatsu's planned November 5 sailing from Galway.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy states that Takamatsu had applied at the U.S. Consulate General in London and hoped to spend about a month in the United States. Because wartime sailing opportunities were scarce, it requested prompt instructions to the consular officer at Galway.

subfiles.title: Copy of Japanese Embassy memorandum seeking Takamatsu's visa
subfiles.about: Duplicates the request to expedite Takamatsu's temporary visitor's visa.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum repeats that Takamatsu was waiting at Galway for a November 5 vessel and wanted to visit the United States for one month. It emphasizes the difficulty of obtaining passage and asks that the Galway consular officer receive instructions.

subfiles.title: Japanese Embassy memorandum on Takamatsu's arrival aboard the Fushimi Maru
subfiles.about: Requests permission for Takamatsu to remain in the United States for one month after the Fushimi Maru reached New York.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy notes that the desired visa had not been issued before Takamatsu left Galway and that he had been allowed to land temporarily while the ship remained in port. It says he wished to rest and discuss business with his newspaper's New York correspondent.

subfiles.title: Press release publishing Clarke H. Kawakami's resignation letter
subfiles.about: Releases Kawakami's letter resigning from Domei and condemning Japan's attack and militarist government.
subfiles.summary: American-born Domei correspondent Clarke H. Kawakami expresses shock at Japan's attack, accuses its leaders of deception, and says truthful reports from Washington had been withheld from the Japanese public. He supports the defeat of militarism, identifies America as being in the right, and offers to enlist in the U.S. Army after resolving family and financial matters. He also mentions that his father was being held at Gloucester City, New Jersey.

subfiles.title: Telegram on treatment of Japanese correspondents in the United States
subfiles.about: Describes U.S. treatment of Japanese correspondents and requests reciprocal safeguards for American correspondents in Japanese-controlled territory.
subfiles.summary: The Department says that only correspondents suspected of inimical activity had been apprehended and that others remained at liberty locally. Detainees were being investigated promptly and housed comfortably pending release or inclusion in a reciprocal exchange. Bern was instructed to seek Japanese assurances of equivalent treatment for American reporters.

subfiles.title: Follow-up telegram requesting an early Japanese response
subfiles.about: Requests an early reply to the December 24 inquiry about reciprocal treatment of correspondents.
subfiles.summary: The Department cites numerous inquiries about the status of newspapermen. It asks the Legation to expedite a response to its earlier telegram.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on including press representatives in exchanges
subfiles.about: References a proposal that accredited press representatives, radio reporters, and press photographers be included in exchanges on a reciprocal basis.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to telegram 405 in another decimal-file series. Its subject records a broad definition of press personnel eligible for exchange.

subfiles.title: Special Division memorandum on treatment of American newspapermen in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports that no specific information was available on the treatment of American newspapermen in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum quotes the Department's December 24 message asking Japan to guarantee reciprocal good treatment. Pending a reply, it recommends continuing the stated U.S. policy toward Japanese correspondents.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Isamu Suzukawa's possible transfer
subfiles.about: Records a Spanish Embassy inquiry about whether former Asahi correspondent Isamu Suzukawa could go to Hot Springs.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Gortazar was told that the answer depended on whether U.S. authorities were detaining Suzukawa. The sheet refers to a memorandum filed in the exchange series.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Yoshiyuki Akiyama's transfer to Hot Springs
subfiles.about: Records that former Japanese correspondent Yoshiyuki Akiyama had been transferred to Hot Springs on January 23.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies Akiyama as a former news correspondent. It points to the underlying Justice Department document in another file.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference recommending Akiyama's transfer to Hot Springs
subfiles.about: References the view that detained Domei manager Yoshiyuki Akiyama should join other Japanese correspondents at Hot Springs.
subfiles.summary: Akiyama is identified as manager of Domei's San Francisco branch. The recommendation rested on the concentration of other former Japanese newspaper correspondents at Hot Springs.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on an Associated Press request for reciprocal treatment
subfiles.about: Records an inquiry concerning transfer of a Japanese newspaperman from Camp Missoula to the Homestead on reciprocity grounds.
subfiles.summary: Fletcher Warren asked what treatment American newspapermen were receiving in Japan so that the Justice Department could answer an Associated Press request. Keeley replied that the Department had favorable information about Germany and Italy but no specific information about Japan and promised to investigate.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Akiyama's detention at Fort Missoula
subfiles.about: Asks whether the State Department wanted Yoshiyuki Akiyama transferred from Fort Missoula to Hot Springs.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies Akiyama as the claimed manager of Domei's San Francisco branch. It refers to the Justice Department's inquiry in another file.

subfiles.title: Spanish Embassy memorandum concerning Kyozo Mori's automobile
subfiles.about: Requests guidance on Kyozo Mori's proposal to give his automobile to former Asahi employees in New York.
subfiles.summary: Mori wished to reward Larry Tajiri, Robert Tsuda, and Thomas Komuro by transferring his 1940 Ford sedan to Tajiri. The Embassy asked whether the gift was permissible or whether its New York consulate should take possession and eventually sell the car with former Japanese consular vehicles.

subfiles.title: Foreign Funds Control memorandum on Mori and Ichimura
subfiles.about: Advises that Mori could give away his automobile but that transferring its title required a Treasury license.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum recommends telling the Spanish Embassy that the State Department had no objection to the gift. It also discusses Teizo Ichimura, who was ill with tuberculosis at Saranac Lake, and Treasury's request for supporting papers concerning his case.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference listing Japanese newsmen and their newspapers
subfiles.about: Points to a letter listing Japanese newsmen and the newspapers they represented.
subfiles.summary: The sheet contains no list itself. It directs researchers to the original letter in file 894.20211/527.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on exchange of press representatives and dependents
subfiles.about: Records the Department's agreement with a detailed proposal to include press representatives and their dependents in an exchange.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to the underlying communication in the diplomatic-exchange file. Its subject confirms Departmental approval in principle.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese exchange-vessel priorities
subfiles.about: References Japan's proposal that governments agree on priorities for press representatives and other nonofficial persons aboard exchange vessels.
subfiles.summary: The sheet summarizes a Japanese proposal for allocating limited exchange-vessel accommodations. It directs readers to the original document in the exchange file.

subfiles.title: Foreign Activity Correlation routing sheet
subfiles.about: Routes an attached matter among numerous Department divisions.
subfiles.summary: The page consists chiefly of office abbreviations and a March 11 stamp. It appears to have served as the circulation cover for the censorship material that follows.

subfiles.title: National Censorship report on Japanese correspondents' letter to Suzukawa
subfiles.from: Kyozo Mori, Denji Kato, Goro Nakano, and S. Nakamura
subfiles.about: Summarizes a condemned letter from Japanese correspondents at Hot Springs to Isamu Suzukawa in New York.
subfiles.summary: The envelope contained four messages expressing hopes that Suzukawa would soon join the detained correspondents. The writers named other Japanese reporters already together at Hot Springs and referred to Nichi Nichi correspondents and former New York Asahi staff who remained in New York. National Censorship categorized the correspondence as political and Japanese.

subfiles.title: Duplicate National Censorship report on letter to Suzukawa
subfiles.from: Kyozo Mori, Denji Kato, Goro Nakano, and S. Nakamura
subfiles.about: Duplicates the censorship summary of messages sent from Hot Springs to Suzukawa.
subfiles.summary: The copy repeats the correspondents' efforts to arrange for Suzukawa to join them and lists colleagues already in custody. It records that the original letter was condemned rather than released.

subfiles.title: Bern telegram reporting Japan's position on American correspondents
subfiles.about: Reports Japan's assertion that American correspondents received the same treatment as other Americans.
subfiles.summary: The Swiss minister in Tokyo relayed the Japanese Foreign Office's statement that journalists were not being treated worse than other Americans. The report answered the Department's January 23 inquiry about American interests in Japan.

subfiles.title: Departmental reply clarifying treatment of Japanese journalists
subfiles.about: Rejects any suggestion that journalists should receive unfavorable treatment and asks Japan to treat detained American journalists considerately.
subfiles.summary: The Department says detained Japanese journalists were housed with Japanese officials at a hotel and received equivalent comforts, while other journalists remained at liberty. It asks the Japanese Foreign Office to provide corresponding treatment to Americans in Japanese custody.

subfiles.title: Spanish Embassy memorandum requesting repatriation of the Tomomatsus
subfiles.about: Requests that Toshio Tomomatsu and his wife be allowed to join the Japanese official group at Hot Springs.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy identifies Tomomatsu as a Domei correspondent sent from Tokyo to San Francisco in 1939. It gives his Alameda address and asks the Department to consider his request to join the repatriation group.

subfiles.title: Spanish transmittal and intelligence note on Toshio Tomomatsu
subfiles.about: Transmits memoranda on Japanese affairs, including a note describing Tomomatsu's Domei duties and contacts.
subfiles.summary: The attached note identifies Tomomatsu as Yoshiyuki Akiyama's assistant in San Francisco. It states that Domei used commercial wireless receivers to obtain pro-Japanese news from Japan and sold the material to two Japanese-language newspapers.

subfiles.title: State Department response concerning the Tomomatsus
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the request for Mr. and Mrs. Tomomatsu to join the official Japanese party at Hot Springs.
subfiles.summary: The Department recognizes that the Tomomatsus were eligible for repatriation with the official party. The surviving text ends before the Department's complete determination of their request is stated.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on repatriation priorities for press representatives
subfiles.about: References a telegram concerning repatriation of press representatives and their families and the priority assigned among unofficial Japanese.
subfiles.summary: The OCR of the subject is damaged, but it clearly concerns correspondents and their families within repatriation priorities. The sheet points to telegram 665 in the exchange file.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on transferring three Japanese newspapermen
subfiles.about: References a request to transfer Isamu Suzukawa, Tokumaru Nishijima, and Toichiro Takamatsu to White Sulphur Springs.
subfiles.summary: The men are identified respectively with the Tokyo and Osaka Asahi and the Tokyo Nichi Nichi. The sheet points to the original request in the Pacific War file.

subfiles.title: Spanish Embassy memorandum forwarding Kyozo Mori's property request
subfiles.about: Forwards Mori's request for the return or formal accounting of personal property allegedly taken by U.S. authorities.
subfiles.summary: Before sailing on the Gripsholm, Mori listed notebooks, diaries, family letters and films, scrapbooks, a checkbook, and manuscripts missing from his New York residence and Asahi office. He believed the FBI might hold them and requested either their return or a formal statement ensuring their postwar recovery. The Embassy sought an early reply.

subfiles.title: Note to the Treasury concerning Mori's missing property
subfiles.about: Transmits the Spanish Embassy memorandum and FBI response and asks whether Treasury had a record of Mori's missing articles.
subfiles.summary: The note encloses memorandum no. 285 and a July 22 letter from J. Edgar Hoover. It seeks Treasury assistance in locating or documenting articles allegedly removed from Mori's residence and office.

subfiles.title: Note to the Attorney General concerning Mori's missing property
subfiles.about: Asks the FBI to determine whether it had records or receipts for articles allegedly taken from Kyozo Mori.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwards the Spanish Embassy's June 25 memorandum concerning Mori, who had recently left aboard the Gripsholm. It requests any relevant receipts so they could be transmitted to the protecting power.

subfiles.title: Interim reply to the Spanish Embassy on Mori's property
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Mori's property claim and states that the Department was seeking receipts.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes that Mori had been repatriated aboard the Gripsholm. It promises to transmit any receipts obtained from U.S. authorities to the Embassy.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Axis nationals seeking to remain in the United States
subfiles.about: Reviews requests by members of Axis official parties to remain in the United States and the risk of retaliation against American correspondents.
subfiles.summary: Warren lists German, Hungarian, Italian, and other Axis nationals assembled at the Greenbrier Hotel and distinguishes Paul Scheffer, Robert Minner, and Leo Rea as cases likely to provoke their governments. He recalls a German warning that Associated Press correspondent Louis Lochner might be imprisoned if Scheffer were not included in the German party. The memorandum considers illness or omission from final exchange lists as possible ways to let the three remain, while acknowledging the danger of reprisals.

subfiles.title: Treasury report and enclosures concerning Mori's missing effects
subfiles.about: Reports Treasury's investigation into property allegedly missing from Mori's residence and Asahi office and encloses Federal Reserve Bank records.
subfiles.summary: Treasury states that its agents never entered Mori's residence but secured the Asahi office from December 7 to 15, 1941, after which records were stored by the Federal Reserve Bank. Army intelligence and FBI personnel entered the office on December 17, but Captain Stewart Murray denied taking the listed articles; Treasury therefore had no information locating them. Enclosures document the later receipt of magazines, newspapers, cartons of effects, and possession of the office by Isamu Suzukawa and Edna E. Bush.

subfiles.title: Final memorandum to the Spanish Embassy on Mori's missing articles
subfiles.about: Reports that no appropriate U.S. agency had a record of the articles Mori claimed were taken.
subfiles.summary: The Department refers to its July 9 acknowledgment of the Spanish Embassy's request. It states that neither the FBI nor any other relevant government agency could account for the listed property from Mori's New York residence and office.
